subject: physics_2
question_text: What happens to compass needles at the Earth's poles?

verification.note: Asked in a Telangana IPE paper: the book prints the citation '(Mar 17 TS)' beside this question — March 2017. The appearances schema carries year and board but no month field, so March is recorded here; the question number is not printed. The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: at the magnetic poles the dip is 90°, the field is vertical and its horizontal component is zero, so a compass needle pivoted in the horizontal plane feels no aligning torque and settles in no particular direction; a needle free to turn in a vertical plane stands vertical — the book words this as the needle aligning perpendicular to the earth's surface.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Field at the poles
lines: At the earth's magnetic poles the field is
vertical. The angle of dip is 90°, so the
horizontal component of the field is zero.
steps.margin_note: First mark. State the field there: vertical, dip 90°, horizontal component zero.
steps.why: Everything the needle does follows from the field's direction. At the poles the total field points straight into or out of the ground, so the horizontal part — the only part a flat compass can use — vanishes.
common_mistakes: Saying the field is strongest at the poles instead of saying it is vertical. The direction, not the strength, is what answers this question.
Writing dip = 0° at the poles. Dip is 90° at the poles and 0° at the magnetic equator.

recall.must_convey: That at the magnetic poles the earth's field is vertical, the dip is 90° and the horizontal component is zero.
accept: the field is vertical at the poles

steps.memory_tip: At the poles the field goes straight down (or up): dip 90°, nothing left for the horizontal.

steps.label: The needle's behaviour
lines: A compass needle turns in the horizontal
plane. With no horizontal component there
is no torque to set its direction, so the
needle can rest pointing any way — it
shows no useful direction at the poles.
A needle free to turn in a vertical plane
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two behaviours: the flat compass loses its direction; a vertically pivoted needle stands straight up and down.
steps.why: The book words this as the needle aligning perpendicular to the earth's surface — that is what a needle free to tilt in a vertical plane does, since only the vertical component remains. A compass pivoted flat cannot tilt, so what it shows is a needle with no set direction.
common_mistakes: Saying the compass points to the geographic pole. With zero horizontal field it points nowhere in particular.
Saying the flat compass needle turns vertical. A horizontally pivoted needle cannot tilt — only a vertically pivoted one stands vertical.

recall.must_convey: That with zero horizontal component the compass needle has no set direction, while a vertically pivoted needle stands vertical.
accept: the needle can rest any way

steps.memory_tip: A flat compass reads only the horizontal field — at the poles that is zero, so it has nothing to read.

insider_note: The question as asked in 2017 needs the mechanism, not just the fact — zero horizontal component, therefore no torque, therefore no direction.
